st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s public-centred governance logic and materially develops it by explaining why court-led doctrine can reflect resource-skewed disputes, favouring deliberate legislative policymaking and active lawyer participation. Its enterprise-governance discussion extends beyond the court-specific synthesis but does not conflict with it.
qs: We only get court opinions when institutional actors with resources can afford to bring cases.
There’s a reason another branch of government is elected by the public and is designed to actually deliberate over what regulation should look like.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s account of protection and accountability risks by providing a concrete self-representation episode involving allegedly purposeless AI-generated filings, substantial defense costs and a fabricated authority. qs: One especially interesting detail is that somewhere in all of the documents ChatGPT produced, there was a hallucinated case cite—the phrase that strikes fear in the heart of lawyers.
Stanford CodeX has argued that the better framing may be product liability—that OpenAI built a system in a way that allowed users to cross the threshold from information to advice.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source accepts the practitioner-led case for engaging with AI before technological certainty and materially develops its governance dimension. It argues that lawyers must participate in regulatory design, while responsibility should extend beyond users to model developers and downstream legal-AI vendors; its claims remain argumentative and anecdotal rather than outcome-based.
qs: Lawyers are needed to help figure out what the regulation should be.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

It materially extends the cluster by advocating governance-led experimentation that builds institutional memory, highlighting legal-first enterprise rollout, and identifying dependencies on application and frontier-model providers, while treating ROI and adoption claims cautiously.
qs: This is a massive change-management project across the whole relationship between firms and corporate legal departments.

kp.k: AI automates tailored monitoring, but human attention remains limiting
kp.d: McCormack describes using Claude Pro’s Co-work to build a tracker that regularly sweeps domestic court decisions, legislation, regulation, enterprise adoption and agentic commerce, translating developments into her particular work priorities. She compares its output to several full-time research assistants, but this is a personal experience rather than measured productivity evidence. Both hosts identify setup, continually changing features and absorbing outputs as persistent human bottlenecks.
qs: I could imagine having a few research assistants working on that full time.
It doesn’t help much if it produces something really interesting and I never use it or even process it.
The setup itself takes time, and then there’s a new feature, or a new tool, or a new workflow, and suddenly you’re off in another direction.

kp.k: Small-business analysis illustrates expanded access to professional capabilities
kp.d: Leonard reports uploading two years of company books plus year-to-date information to Co-work, receiving revenue and profit analysis, a three-year monthly heat map and marketing recommendations. She treats this as an analogy to legal services: AI supplies analysis that would otherwise require time and money to obtain externally. Her estimate that concurrent tasks return 90 percent complete is anecdotal, not a validated performance measure.
qs: But I uploaded our books for the last two years plus the year-to-date information, and I asked it to give me a sense of strong-revenue periods versus weak-revenue periods.
It’s similar to legal, and similar to the topic we’re going to talk about later, in the sense that I don’t otherwise have access to that kind of analysis.
I’ll set it to do five different things at once, go take the dog for a walk, and come back to something that’s 90 percent of the way there.

kp.k: OpenAI lawsuit challenges personalized advice and automated litigation
kp.d: Leonard recounts Nippon Life Insurance Company of America v. OpenAI as a potentially first-impression case. In her account, Graciela Dela Torre settled a disability dispute with counsel in 2024, then used ChatGPT to question her lawyer’s conduct, attempt reopening and generate a new lawsuit plus 44 subsequent motions, subpoenas and filings. Leonard reports a nonexistent case citation and court findings that many filings lacked legitimate purpose. Nippon seeks $300,000 compensatory and $10 million punitive damages, alleging tortious interference, abuse of process and unauthorized practice of law under Illinois law; the transcript reports allegations and events, not a determination of OpenAI’s liability.
qs: But when that happened, the AI drafted an entirely new lawsuit against Nippon Life and then created 44 subsequent motions, subpoenas, and filings in that matter.
Many of those filings, the court found, served no legitimate purpose in the proceedings.
the company is seeking $300,000 in compensatory damages and $10 million in punitive damages.
The theory is that ChatGPT was essentially providing personalized legal advice and drafting litigation documents without a license.

kp.k: Extending human-oriented UPL statutes to chatbots remains contested
kp.d: McCormack questions whether existing state UPL statutes extend to a technology interface rather than a person. She speculates that proposed New York legislation expressly addressing chatbots posing as licensed professionals could signal perceived gaps in existing law. Leonard reports Stanford CodeX’s alternative product-liability framing; neither speaker presents these interpretations as resolved legal findings.
qs: Stanford CodeX has argued that the better framing may be product liability—that OpenAI built a system in a way that allowed users to cross the threshold from information to advice.
But it makes me wonder whether the New York legislation is itself a signal that the legislature doesn’t think UPL statutes naturally extend to chatbots
So can you extend a UPL statute to a technology interface? That feels like a significant stretch to me.

kp.k: UPL remedies could address repeated AI-generated litigation
kp.d: McCormack suggests that UPL offers Nippon strategic advantages through declaratory and injunctive relief, potentially addressing a future wave of chatbot-assisted pro se claims rather than proving harm case by case. She contrasts this with tort remedies’ usual retrospective compensation function, while expressly expressing uncertainty about declaratory relief. The anticipated litigation wave is hypothetical, not documented market evidence.
qs: Tort law mostly compensates harm after the fact.
UPL statutes are often specifically designed to support injunctive relief, and I assume declaratory relief as well.
Otherwise you’re proving harm case by case.

kp.k: Disclaimers raise responsibility questions across the AI supply chain
kp.d: Leonard reports that OpenAI changed its terms in October 2025 to discourage reliance on ChatGPT for legal advice, while subsequent tests still elicited advice and document drafting. She characterizes this as responsibility-shifting and reports Nippon’s lawyers treating the change as evidence of knowledge. A NotebookLM-generated podcast raised stronger regulation of major developers; McCormack questions limiting responsibility to frontier labs when downstream legal-AI vendors also sell tools people rely on. She separately clarifies that an individual using AI to understand and act on their own rights is not thereby committing UPL.
qs: OpenAI updated its terms of service in October 2025 to say users should not rely on ChatGPT for legal advice.
But when others tested the platform after that update, it was still providing legal advice and drafting documents.
So why wouldn’t they also bear legal responsibility if they’re producing tools people rely on?

if you’re an individual who can’t afford a lawyer, and you’re sitting in your Claude or ChatGPT account trying to understand your legal rights and responsibilities, and then you act on that, you’re not guilty of UPL.

kp.d: McCormack argues that governing AI through litigation is inadequate because courts address questions selected by institutional actors able to finance cases, rather than deliberating comprehensively about the public’s desired regulatory framework. Both hosts anticipate state differences and possible legislative–judicial tensions over authority to regulate legal practice. They recommend lawyer involvement in shaping regulation, with Leonard describing failure to learn and use AI as surrendering that opportunity.
qs: We only get court opinions when institutional actors with resources can afford to bring cases. So if that becomes your regulatory mechanism, you’re getting a skewed sample of disputes.
Courts answer the question in front of them.
Lawyers are needed to help figure out what the regulation should be.
So there’s this interesting branch collision too.

kp.k: Legalweek signals vendor expansion and new marketing approaches
kp.d: Discussing Legalweek 2026, held March 9 through 12, McCormack reports more vendors and conspicuous expansion by Clio and Harvey. Leonard interprets Harvey’s large advertisements featuring major-firm chief innovation officers as an endorsement strategy borrowed from other industries. These are conference observations about legal-tech vendors and presentation, not quantified market-share findings or claims about alternative legal service providers.
qs: Those giant ads with chief innovation officers from major firms effectively endorsing Harvey felt like athlete endorsements.
there are new entrants here who think very differently from the incumbents and who are borrowing presentation tactics from other industries.
there were definitely more vendors than ever.

kp.k: ROI scrutiny increases before transformation is clearly demonstrated
kp.d: McCormack reports Danielle Benecke’s sequence of discovery in 2023, experimentation in 2024, workflow deployment in 2025 and value scrutiny in 2026, while noting some firms remained experimental in 2025 and that Benecke may be describing rather than endorsing the ROI focus. McCormack cautions against narrow immediate-return measures. Leonard says she heard urgency but found no clear, compelling firm-level ROI account, attributing the difficulty to inconsistent usage and extensive change management across firms and corporate legal departments.
qs: 2023 as the year of discovery, 2024 as experimentation, 2025 as the year we started to see real deployment in legal workflows, and 2026 as the year value is under the microscope.
I think it’s a mistake to think about this too narrowly in immediate ROI terms.
the theme was definitely ROI, but I didn’t leave with any clear answers to the ROI question.
Even getting people to use AI more consistently is still a challenge.

kp.k: Reported in-house adoption surge carries unresolved methodological questions
kp.d: McCormack cites a Relativity statistic that generative-AI adoption among corporate legal departments rose from 44 percent to 87 percent in a single year, interpreting it as consistent with in-house leadership. Leonard explicitly says she has not examined the methodology and questions department size and whether adoption means actual usage or merely available licenses. She contrasts the headline figure with conversations with smaller corporate legal teams that have done little. The transcript provides no survey sample size or precise comparison years for this statistic.
qs: generative AI adoption among corporate legal departments jumping from 44 percent to 87 percent in a single year.
I’d want to know what size departments were surveyed and what they mean by “adoption.”
Are we talking about actual usage? Or are we talking about licenses purchased and made available?
Because we talk to a lot of corporate counsel, especially at smaller organizations, who have done very little for understandable reasons.

kp.k: Pricing discussions expose revenue concerns and risk-allocation difficulties
kp.d: Leonard predicts firms are unlikely to see revenue gains yet and describes many as hoping to avoid revenue losses. She observes increasing pricing conversations and compares them to Great Recession debates over alternative fee arrangements, litigation volumes and changing scopes. She suggests professional risk aversion helps explain reluctance to allocate risks despite detailed time records. McCormack notes the differing incentives of in-house cost centers and law-firm revenue centers.
qs: And you’re probably not going to see revenue gains yet. A lot of firms are really hoping not to see revenue losses.
Pricing conversations are definitely picking up from what I’m seeing.
But it reminds me of the old conversations we had during the Great Recession around AFAs—who’s going to bear the risk of more litigation, less litigation, changing scopes, all of it.
Cost center versus revenue center matters there too.

kp.k: Agentic systems increase attention to layered governance responsibilities
kp.d: Leonard identifies a shift from chatbots to agentic systems as a major conference theme, while acknowledging Legalweek’s AI-strategy audience may amplify it. McCormack’s governance panel included Freshfields’ Anna R. Gressel, OpenAI’s Galia Amram and Moderna’s Henry Hagen, all working directly with frontier-model infrastructure. She notes the absence of an intermediary such as Harvey or Legora and speculates that some buyers prefer those vendors partly to outsource governance work; this is a perceived buyer benefit, not an established transfer of legal responsibility.
qs: The other big theme this year was the shift from chatbots to agentic systems, which is happening whether people fully realize it or not.
It matters how the underlying model companies think about governance, and frankly how good their governance actually is, because people are counting on it.
a lot of legal buyers may actually prefer to outsource part of their governance burden to a company like Harvey or Legora.

kp.k: Legal-first adoption can enable wider enterprise deployment
kp.d: McCormack reports that Moderna began enterprise adoption of OpenAI products with its legal team. She regards that sequencing as a way for lawyers to understand risks and safe uses before wider rollout, enabling rather than merely slowing the business. This is a reported organizational example and her interpretation of its mechanism, not a measured comparison with other adoption strategies.
qs: Moderna has been early to enterprise adoption of OpenAI’s products across the business, but they started with the legal team.
you want the legal team to understand the trap doors and the safe lanes first.
If legal figures that out early, it allows the rest of the business to move faster.

kp.k: Governance requires iterative participation rather than waiting
kp.d: McCormack reports panel consensus that inaction poses greater risks than proceeding with imperfect governance and that waiting to be a fast follower is not viable. Leonard argues that active governance develops institutional memory through learning what works, even as systems evolve faster than frameworks. These are recommendations and risk judgments, not empirical findings. McCormack mentions an AAA survey of 500 C-suite leaders on AI governance as ongoing work, without presenting results.
qs: the AAA is doing this large survey of 500 C-suite leaders about where they are on AI governance.
yes, governance is hard; yes, it’s tricky; yes, it’s imperfect everywhere. But the bigger risk is doing nothing.
Even if the framework is imperfect, and even if the systems are moving faster than governance can keep up, you’re still building institutional memory.
One of the themes on the panel was that waiting to be a fast follower isn’t really an option here.

kp.k: AI governance creates advisory opportunities for lawyers
kp.d: Leonard describes AI governance guidance as a potential revenue and service opportunity for law firms. McCormack supports the demand claim with anecdotal reports of lawyers seeking informal help constructing governance frameworks. Their account suggests expanding legal advisory work around organizational AI adoption, without quantifying market size or realized revenue.
qs: We get a lot of calls from lawyers who basically want us to act as informal advisors while they’re trying to build governance frameworks.
this is a real source of revenue and service.
There’s so much demand for this kind of guidance.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The speakers describe AI expanding research and analytical capacity, creating litigation and regulatory risks, shifting legal buyers toward agentic systems, and generating demand for governance advice, while law-firm returns remain unclear.
pts.d: McCormack reports that Claude built a self-updating AI-governance tracker that categorizes developments and translates them for her AAA work and other activities; she compares its capacity to several full-time research assistants. Leonard reports using Co-work for small-business financial analysis she otherwise would not readily obtain. Both identify human attention, setup and processing of outputs as continuing constraints. In Leonard's account of Nippon Life v. OpenAI, ChatGPT supplied personalized advice and litigation documents, including a fabricated citation, enabling renewed litigation after a settlement. These are reported allegations and case circumstances, not an adjudicated finding that OpenAI practiced law. McCormack questions whether statutes written for people extend to chatbots; she argues that a successful UPL theory could provide a route to injunctions against recurring AI-generated litigation. She anticipates state variation and argues that litigation-driven regulation produces a resource-skewed selection of disputes. Leonard describes a shift from chatbots to agentic systems and observes pricing discussions but no clear, compelling law-firm ROI picture. McCormack interprets Moderna's legal-first adoption as enabling the wider business to move faster and suggests that buyers may use vendors such as Harvey or Legora partly to outsource governance work. Both argue that adopting and governing systems builds institutional learning, while waiting sacrifices it. Leonard identifies AI-governance advice as a revenue and service opportunity for law firms. The discussion also relays external claims about adoption and deployment stages, whose original attribution is preserved in the evidence item.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source primarily offers personal experience, conference observations, a lawsuit narrative and reported panel views, with one externally attributed adoption statistic and no measured productivity or ROI study.
pts.d: The workflow claims rest on the speakers' own use of Claude Co-work; Leonard's statement that outputs are 90 percent complete is an informal assessment, not a benchmark. The litigation discussion draws on documents Leonard says she uploaded into NotebookLM and on its generated podcast. She reports 44 subsequent litigation documents, approximately $300,000 in defense costs claimed by Nippon, a request for $10 million in punitive damages and a hallucinated citation. The potential spread of such litigation over the next year or two is explicitly introduced as a question raised by the NotebookLM-generated podcast, not independent empirical evidence. The alternative product-liability framing is attributed to Stanford CodeX. The adoption increase from 44 percent to 87 percent in one year is attributed to Relativity, not a study conducted by the speakers; Leonard expressly says she did not examine its methodology and questions department sizes and the meaning of adoption. The discovery–experimentation–deployment–value sequence is attributed to Baker McKenzie's Danielle Benecke, with McCormack offering qualified agreement. The claim that waiting is riskier than moving is reported as a consensus of McCormack's panel, comprising Anna R. Gressel, Galia Amram and Henry Hagen; the transcript supplies no quantified risk comparison. McCormack's AAA survey of 500 C-suite leaders is ongoing work, not reported results. Demand for governance services is supported by calls the speakers receive and their planned educational project, not market-sizing data.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion concerns conditions around Legalweek 2026; broader litigation growth and mature agentic governance remain prospective and uncertain.
pts.d: The workflow examples are current personal experiences in 2026. McCormack's tracker currently covers domestic developments, and its proposed email delivery is an anticipated capability she has not yet requested. The lawsuit narrative places the settlement in 2024 and OpenAI's terms update in October 2025; the outcome of the lawsuit remains unknown. The next-year-or-two litigation scenario comes from the generated podcast and is presented as a possibility. McCormack's injunction argument expressly depends on success of the UPL claim, and her regulatory expectations depend on differences among state statutes and the roles of courts and legislatures. Benecke's reported sequence spans 2023–2026, but McCormack notes that some firms remained in experimentation during 2025. Leonard frames law-firm ROI and revenue gains as not yet clearly demonstrable, rather than permanently unavailable, given inconsistent usage and substantial change-management requirements. She qualifies the adoption statistic by distinguishing actual use from purchased licenses and pointing to smaller departments with limited adoption. The benefits of early governance depend on active experimentation, attention and iterative learning; neither speaker claims that a settled model of strong agentic governance already exists.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern individual legal users, corporate defendants and in-house teams, law firms, technology providers, regulators and small-business users.
pts.d: Individuals unable to afford lawyers may use general-purpose AI to understand rights and responsibilities; McCormack explicitly distinguishes this self-help from the individual committing UPL. The case narrative illustrates possible harm from personalized chatbot advice, while the speakers question disclaimers that transfer responsibility to users. Corporate defendants and their in-house counsel could face additional defense costs if chatbot-assisted claims proliferate. In-house departments face adoption and governance demands, with differences between large and small organizations and between cost-center and revenue-center incentives. Law firms face uncertain financial returns, pricing and risk-allocation discussions, and new client-service opportunities in AI governance and regulatory design. Frontier-model companies and downstream legal-tech vendors face questions about product responsibility; McCormack rejects assuming that only major model developers should bear it. Courts and legislatures face differing jurisdictional and institutional roles in setting boundaries. McCormack's own research workflow illustrates expanded capacity for institutional leaders, but does not establish actual research-assistant job losses. Leonard's small-business example concerns access to financial analysis rather than civil access to justice.
